newsitem.title: UK: UK taxes can be cut by two billion stg - think tank.
newsitem.headline: UK taxes can be cut by two billion stg - think tank.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has room to cut UK income tax to the tune of two billion pounds, matched by reductions in public spending plans, the Centre for Economic Forecasting said on Friday.
That would allow Clarke to cut around a penny off the basic rate of income tax at his November 26 budget, taking it to 23 percent.
The Centre also said fears of a consumer boom fuelling inflationary pressures were misplaced. It forecast consumer spending will increase by 3.9 percent next year, having risen 3.0 percent in 1996.
That will help UK economic growth rise from 2.5 percent this year to 3.3 percent in 1997, the Centre said. But it said growth would then drop back to 2.8 percent in 1998.

Andrew Sentance, director of the Centre for Economic Forecasting at the London Business School, said tax cuts of more than 2.0 billion stg in November could only be afforded through higher indirect taxes or duties on less sensitive areas such as tobacco, airport duty and insurance tax.
But looking to the medium-term, he said Britain appears to have reached the end of the tax-cutting road.

Sentance said Britain's public sector deficit was unlikely to move into surplus by the end of the century, as the last budget projections implied. Instead it is likely to fall to around 1.5 percent of GDP.
That sort of deficit is sustainable, he said, but left little leeway if the economy is hit by recession or external shock.
As a result, further tax cuts in the medium-term could only be justified if the lost revenue was raised in some other way, perhaps through reform to the welfare state.
"But the timescale for reform in this area is very long and a strong political commitment to change is needed." he said.
The Centre also forecast UK underlying inflation would stay slightly above the government's target of 2.5 percent. But subdued wage growth is expected to keep it below 3.0 percent.

"In the short-term, the strength of sterling, the weakness of factory gate prices and rapidly declining inflation in the food sector will help to keep down inflation, offsetting the impact of recent increases in petrol prices," the report said.

The Centre said the UK economy would benefit from factors other than higher consumer spending next year. "Investment growth is also forecast to strengthen and the UK should benefit from an improving world economic situation, particularly in continental Europe," the report said.
